subject: Error in null model with no covariates

messages.author: 036659353a33b729
messages.subject: Error in null model with no covariates
parts:
Hello all,

Previously I developed an unmarkedFrameOccu using covariates and i had no issue as below:

occ <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = dethist, 
                             siteCovs = site_covariates, 
                             obsCovs = NULL)  # because there are not survey-level covariates 

But, today I am using another data set with only detection history with no data for covariates. For this i created the unmarkedFrameOccu object as below:
umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=data1)

then i created the null model as below:
null <- occu(~1 ~1, umf,) 
this returned error as "Error: Hessian is singular.  Try providing starting values or using fewer covariates."

then i tried to use the below models using start and se:
null <- occu(~1 ~1, umf, starts=c(1,0))
null <- occu(~1 ~1, umf, se=F)

Using the above two starts and se, the model ran with no error. 
They gave same detection estimates but the SE, Z and other values came out as NA. Further the occupancy estimates differed in both estimates. 

Then i tried to swap the starts=c(1,0) to starts=c(0,1) and and this gave the same error as this model null <- occu(~1 ~1, umf,) 

My questions are:

1. Firstly why does this error arise? Is it due to too little data or too many data? (# of observations). For this data set I had 34 rows and 123 columns
2. why is a starting value needed? And does the sequence of 0, 1 matter ? 
3. What is the suggested approach to deal with such issues? 

Your support and inputs will be highly appreciated.

Dechen

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Error in null model with no covariates
parts:
Hi Dechen,

Your questions hit on some of the mechanics of maximum likelihood estimation--I'll give this a shot, but there are certainly many other people on the board whom are better equipped to answer.
  • The principle behind MLE is that the best guess for a parameter value theta is that value of theta for which pr(data|theta) is greatest. In practice, your computer is using some algorithm to iteratively guess at values of theta until it finds those values where pr(data|theta) is greatest. Sometimes, the computer doesn't quite do as well as one would like. For example, it might explore some wildly incorrect part of the possible parameter space and converge upon some local optima (a combination of values for which the likelihood is greater than nearby combinations of parameter values); it might explore some wildly incorrect part of the possible parameter space where all guesses are extremely and nearly equivalently unlikely and ultimately give up and provide some convergence error. These issues can be more likely to occur if the algorithm starts its sequences of guesses in said bad part of the parameter space, and entering arguments for starting values is one way to make sure the algorithm at least starts its guesses with plausible values. Maybe the easiest way to specify starting values is to look at the the estimates from a similar/nested model using the same data.
  • Re. the sequence and specific values used: for a occu model ~1~1, one value corresponds to p on the logit scale, and one to psi on the logit scale because this is the link function used(I don't remember whether detection or occupancy comes first). The inverse logit of 0 or 1 respectively equals 0.5 or about 0.7, for what it's worth: these might or might not be realistic starting values for what you've got.
  • The variance covariance matrix and standard errors are derived from the Hessian matrix, which is based on second deriviatives of the likelihood w/ respect to the parameters (if there's a really pronounced maxima w/r/t some parameter, the SE is smaller). If you specify se=FALSE, than the call to occu does not include calculating the Hessian, and so both you avoid any error about it being singular and cannot estimate standard errors
  • Calculation of the Hessian is more difficult and can fail when the model is very complex (overfit) or if the optimizer ends up on some ridge in the likelihood, hence the error message.
As to what is triggering the error with your data...completely speculating, but perhaps p is very low?

Cheers,

John

messages.subject: Re: Error in null model with no covariates
parts:
Hi John,

Been a while since this thread was active but hopefully someone out there is listening! 

I've also come across the Hessian is singular error for a few of my species that I'm trying to get detection probability from. I'm not using any covariates: occu(~1 ~1, data = WGK), where WGK is the unmarkedFrameOccu output. Your last point above is interesting - the output from occu gives me an NA for p, but if I add a couple of hundred rows of zeros to the detection data p is 0 and I don't get the Hessian error. I'm wondering if there is therefore an issue of overfit? And if so, what's the way around that?

Thanks
Simeon

messages.author: 6ad895aa93bfdc63
messages.subject: Re: Error in null model with no covariates
parts:
Hi Simeon,

I don't fully understand what you are reporting--the SE was NA using the actual data, but the SE (or the coefficient? backtransformed coefficient?) was 0 after padding the actual data with hundreds of fake 0's?  What do the other coefficients/SE look like? Depending upon how you choose to look at it, a hessian error when fitting the null model could either be a poor omen, or a happy indicator that you may have more time available to consider other things. 

John
